notes.text: The killing and eating of the paschal lamb, ver. 1-6, 8-11.
The sprinkling of the blood upon the doorposts, peculiar to the first passover, ver. 7. with the reason for it, ver. 11-13.

The feast of unleavened bread for seven days after; this points rather at what was to be done after in the observance of this ordinance, ver. 14-20. This institution is communicated to the people, and they instructed in the observance. (1.) Of this first passover, ver. 21-23. (2.) Of the after passovers, ver. 24-27. And the Israelites obedience to these orders, ver. 28. II. None of all the providences of God concerning the Jewish church was more illustrious, than the deliverance of the children of Israel out of Egypt.

1. The first-born of the Egyptians are slain, ver. 29, 30.

2. Orders are given immediately for their discharge, ver. 31-33.

3. They begin their march,

1. Loaded with their own effects, ver. 34.

2. Enriched with the spoils of Egypt, ver. 35, 36.

3. Attended with a mixed multitude, ver. 37, 38,

4. Put to their shifts for present supply, ver. 39. This event is dated, ver. 40-42. III. A recapitulation in the close, 1st. Of this memorable ordinance, with some additions, ver. 43-49; 2ndly. Of this memorable providence, ver. 50, 51.

1. The Lord spake - Had spoken, before the three days darkness. But the mention of it was put off to this place, that the history of the plagues might not be interrupted.

2. This shall be to you the beginning of months - They had hitherto begun their year from the middle of September, but hence-forward they were to begin it from the middle of March, at least in all their ecclesiastical computations. We may suppose that while Moses was bringing the ten plagues upon the Egyptians, he was directing the Israelites to prepare for their departure at an hour's warning. Probably he had, by degrees, brought them near together from their dispersions, for they are here called the congregation of Israel; and to them, as a congregation, orders are here sent.

3. Take every man a lamb - In each of their families, or two or three families, if they were small, join for a lamb. The lamb was to be got ready four days before. and that afternoon they went, they were to kill it, (ver. 6,) as a sacrifice, not strictly, for it was not offered upon the altar, but as a religious ceremony, acknowledging God's goodness to them, not only in preserving them from, but in delivering them by the plagues inflicted on the Egyptians. The lamb so slain they were to eat roasted (we may suppose in its several quarters) with unleavened bread and bitter herbs; they were to eat it in haste, ver. 11, and to leave none of it until the morning; for God would have them to depend upon him for their daily bread. Before they eat the flesh of the lamb, they were to sprinkle the blood upon the door-posts; by which their houses were to be distinguished from the houses of the Egyptians, and so their first-born secured from the sword of the destroying angel. Dreadful work was to be made this night in Egypt; all the first-born both of man and beast were to be slain; and judgment executed upon the gods of Egypt, Num. xxxiii, 4. It is probable the idols which the Egyptians worshipped were defaced, those of metal melted, those of wood consumed, and those of stone broke to pieces. This was to be annually observed as a feast of the Lord in their generations, to which the feast of unleavened bread was annexed, during which, for seven days, they were to eat no bread but what was unleavened, in remembrance of their being confined to such bread for many days after they came out of Egypt, ver. 14- 20. There was much of the gospel in this ordinance: (1.) The paschal lamb was typical. Christ is our passover, 1 Cor. v, 7, and is the Lamb of God, John i, 29. 2. It was to be a male of the first year; in its prime. Christ offered up himself in the midst of his days. It notes the strength and sufficiency of the Lord Jesus, on whom our help was laid. 3. It was to be without blemish, noting the purity of the Lord Jesus, a lamb without spot, 1 Pet. i, 19. 4. It was to be set apart four days before, noting the designation of the Lord Jesus to be a saviour, both in the purpose and in the promise. It is observable, that as Christ was crucified at the passover, so he solemnly entered into Jerusalem four days before, the very day that the paschal lamb was set apart. 5. It was to be slain and roasted with fire, noting the exquisite sufferings of the Lord Jesus, even unto death, the death of the cross. 6. It was to be killed by the whole congregation between the two evenings, that is, between three o'clock and six. Christ suffered in the latter end of the world, Heb. ix, 26, by the hand of the Jews, the whole multitude of them, Luke xxiii, 18. 7. Not a bone of it must be broken, ver. 46, which is expressly said to be fulfilled in Christ, John xix, 33, 36. (2.) The sprinkling of the blood was typical. 1st, It was not enough that the blood of the lamb was shed, but it must be sprinkled, noting the application of the merits of Christ's death to our souls; 2ndly, It was to be sprinkled upon the door-posts, noting the open profession we are to make of faith in Christ, and obedience to him. The mark of the beast may be received in the forehead, or in the right hand, but the seal of the lamb is always in the forehead, Rev. vii, 3. 3rdly, The blood thus sprinkled was a means of the preservation of the Israelites from the destroying angel. If the blood of Christ be sprinkled upon our consciences, it will be our protection from the wrath of God, the curse of the law, and the damnation of hell. (3.) The solemn eating of the lamb was typical of our gospel duty to Christ. 1st, The paschal lamb was killed not to be looked upon only, but to be fed upon; so we must by faith make Christ ours, as we do that which we eat, and we must receive spiritual strength and nourishment from him, as from our food, and have delight in him, as we have in eating and drinking when we are hungry or thirsty. 2ndly, It was to be all eaten: those that, by faith, feed upon Christ, must feed upon a whole Christ. They must take Christ and his yoke, Christ and his cross, as well as Christ and his crown. 3rdly, It was to be eaten with bitter herbs, in remembrance of the bitterness of their bondage in Egypt; we must feed upon Christ with brokenness of heart, in remembrance of sin. 4thly, It was to be eaten in a departing posture ver. 11, when we feed upon Christ by faith, we must sit loose to the world, and every thing in it. (4.) The feast of unleavened bread was typical of the Christian life, 1 Cor. v, 7, 8. Having received Christ Jesus the Lord, 1st. We must keep a feast, in holy joy, continually delighting ourselves in Christ Jesus; If true believers have not a continual feast, it is their own fault. 2ndly, It must be a feast of unleavened bread, kept in charity, without the leaven of malice, and in sincerity, without the leaven of hypocrisy. All the old leaven of sin must be put far from us, with the utmost caution, if we would keep the feast of a holy life to the honour of Christ. 3rdly, It was to be an ordinance forever. As long as we live we must continue feeding upon Christ, and rejoicing in him always, with thankful mention of the great things he has done for us.
Raw — Half roasted, but throughly drest.
Ye shall burn with fire — To prevent the profane abuse of it.
The Lord's passover — A sign of his passing over you, when he destroyed the Egyptians.

glossa.text:
*This month,* etc. ((RAB.)) This is April, which among the Hebrews is called Nisam, among the Macedonians Ξανθικός; and it is called *Aprilis* as it were *aperilis*, because then the earth is opened for the bringing forth of shoots, herbs and flowers: or *Aprilis* from Venus, as it were *Aphroditis*; for Venus in Greek is called *Aphrodite*. The Hebrews hold this month as the first, because the fifteenth of its Kalends was the first day of the world: the fourteenth, the second day; the thirteenth, the third; the twelfth, the fourth, on which the sun and the moon were made, and then was the first equinox; for the sun in the east and the moon in the west divided the sphere of the world equally.

((STRAB.)) This is Nisan, according to the Hebrews, in which the world was made, whose full moon is always to be looked for after the vernal equinox: in which the people of Israel is freed from the servitude of Egypt, and the human race is snatched by the blood of Christ from the power of the devil. On the tenth day of the month the lamb is taken, on the fourteenth it is sacrificed: because in the law the passion of Christ is figured, and, the grace of the Gospel flashing forth, it is fulfilled; for the number ten, because of the decalogue, signifies the law, but the number four the four gospels.

*And it shall be,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 42 in Exod., tom. III.)) That manner of speech may disturb a man, etc., *as far as* what was figured by that precept.

*According to which rite,* etc. *Allegorically.* Because Christ took flesh of the just and of sinners, that no one might despair of pardon. Or because Christ was a kid to the Jews, who said: *This man is a sinner (Joan. IX)*, but to us a lamb without spot. Or because he appeared *in the likeness of sinful flesh* and *died for sin, whereas he had no sin ((I Petr. II))*.

((STRAB.)) On the tenth day of April he came to Jerusalem, and on the following day he was received by the crowds with branches of palms and with divine praises. Through the three remaining days he was watched by the Jews until the fourteenth day, that is, until the fifth day of the week, on which he supped with the apostles, and afterwards was betrayed.

*And they shall take of the blood thereof,* etc. ((GREG., homil. 22 in Evang., tom. II.)) The blood is set on when it is drunk not only with the mouth of the body, but also with the mouth of the heart, etc., *as far as* because we bear the cross of his passion upon the forehead.

*And they shall eat the flesh,* etc. ((GREG., ibid.)) By night we eat the lamb, etc., *as far as* for he offers praise out of leaven who prepares for God a sacrifice out of rapine.

*With wild lettuces,* etc. ((GREG., ibid.)) Wild lettuces are exceeding bitter, etc., *as far as* that he may know that all things are dispensed through the power of the Holy Spirit.

*The head with the feet,* etc. *((GREG., ibid.)) The head of Christ is God ((I Cor. XI))*. To devour therefore the head of the lamb, etc., *as far as* let no one be sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the fatherland.

((GREG. NYSS., de Vita Mosis. )) By those wrappings of things he admonishes us that through these riddles we should be willing to consider and to understand that this our life is a certain passing over. For after we have entered upon it, we are always driven by a certain necessity toward the going out, for which he wills us to be prepared with hands and feet and the remaining equipment for the journey. Lest therefore our feet be hurt by thorns on this steep journey of living, we ought to travel not with bare feet, but fortified with harder shoes. But the thorns, which, fixed in the feet, not only hold back and retard but also kill, are sins, from which the hardness of the shoes defends: namely a continent, spare and hard life, which weakens and breaks the points of the thorns, by which, from a small and slender beginning, sins so make their way onward to the things before them, that they slay utterly. To the leading of this life an ankle-length and flowing garment, that is, a voluptuous and vicious manner of living, which lies open most widely, is a hindrance: wherefore it is to be drawn in with a certain girdle and constrained, lest it flow about hither and thither. But the girdle is modesty and a careful manner of living, which admonishes us to use things for necessity, not for pleasure. The staff with which we drive off wild beasts, and by which we are sometimes supported, is hope. But the food set before us is only from the fire, since faith, which is signified by that food, ought to be most burning, possessing nothing moist or slippery.

*Phase.* In Hebrew it is *Pesach* פסח , in Greek Πάσχα, that is, *a passing over;* because it was first celebrated by the children of Israel as they went out of Egypt: we also must pass over from things transitory to things eternal, from things earthly to things heavenly.

*In all the gods,* etc. The Hebrews report that all the idols of Egypt were broken in pieces on that night, and the temples also, either by an earthquake or by an inundation of the river Nile. But allegorically, as we go out of Egypt, the idols of errors fall down, and all the cultivation of perverse doctrines is shaken.

*And you shall have this day,* etc. *((AUG., in Exod. quaest. 43, tom. III.)) And you shall keep this day in your generations as lawful, everlasting* or *eternal;* which in Greek is called αἰὼνιον, is not to be taken thus, etc., *as far as* at every time of the present life simplicity is to be kept, malice to be shunned.

notes.text: The Lord — He rejoiceth over them to do them good. Beautify - Hebrew. adorn, make them amiable and honourable in the eyes of the world, who now hate and despise them. The meek - All true Israelites are such.
In glory — For the honour which God putteth upon them. Beds - By night as well as by day.
Vengeance — For all their cruelties and injuries towards God's people. This was literally accomplished by David upon the Philistines, Ammonites, Syrians and other neighbouring nations.
Written — Appointed and declared in the holy scripture. An exhortation to praise God with all sorts of musical instruments, ver. 1-6.

glossa.text:
*Alleluia.* ((CAS.)) After all the creatures which in the foregoing psalm he admonished to praise God, for that they were created by him, here more properly and more especially he invites Israel to a new canticle for the newness wrought in it, which is the more wonderful working of God: this is the sanctification of Israel, whereby out of the old it was made new.

*Sing ye to the Lord,* etc. ((CAS.)) First in many ways he admonishes them to praise the King who is kind and bountiful *benficus* to them. Secondly he treats of the joys of the saints, there, *They shall rejoice.* ((AUG.)) He that would sing this canticle, let him love things eternal, that he may be made new. For the old man sings an old canticle of earthly things. The new man sings a new one of spiritual things; a canticle, namely, of peace, a canticle *eanticcum* of charity and of gladness. For whosoever follows the old animosity, and not the new charity, sings not a new canticle.

*His praise in the Church.* ((CAS.)) Here he determines where and by whom this canticle ought *debat* to be sung.

*In their king.* ((ID.)) That is, in Christ, who is king and priest. ((AUG.)) As king he fought for us from the cross, overcoming the devil: as priest, he offered himself for us, finding nothing in men that he might offer for them.
*In choir.* ((ID.)) Because there is no dispersion, but a most dear unity; then shall the rejoicing be of the timbrel and the psaltery, not the act of the thing itself.
*For the Lord is well pleased.* ((ID.)) In the first framing of things we read that all things pleased God, etc., *as far as* or when he shall make them equal to the angels.

*The saints shall rejoice.* ((ID.)) The second part, where he treats of the joys of the saints and of their power. *In glory.* It is the frequent praise of good deeds, wherein the just rejoice in their beds, that is, in their conscience, therefore because they have so good a Lord, who gives grace to sinners and eternal life upon their merits. The fool rejoices without, in the tales of men; to the saints this is the manner of joy, that good things be referred to him who gave them.

*Exaltations.* ((ID.)) The strength and power of God is preached in the glory of the saints. In their beds, in the divers mansions, is the glory of the saints. Whereof the Lord says: *In my Father's house there are many mansions *mahsiones*. ((Joan. XIV.))*

*In the throat.* They who in heart and in tongue cease not to praise him from whom they have things eternal.

*Swords.* Receiving the power of the word of God, they shall judge with the Lord, sitting upon twelve seats; and then shall truly be wrought *vengeance and rebuke among the peoples,* then shall the kings of the earth be bound: whence it is free for us to go out *nos*; read *non*, "not". And the nobles shall bear iron fetters, as heavy to carry, and such as cannot be broken: and so shall be wrought the judgment written, that is, approved by the angels. Whereof the Apostle: *Know you not* *Neseitis* *that we shall judge angels? ((I Cor. VI.))* And lest thou think that the apostles alone judge, he adds, *this glory,* that is, the power of judgment, is to all his saints, that is, to the perfect, who for Christ left all earthly things.

((AUG.)) *The exaltations of God in the throat.* For so do they rejoice in their beds and in their throats, that is, in heart and tongue, that they ascribe not to themselves that they are good, but to God, from whom they received what they are, and hope for that which they are not yet.

*To bind.* With these bonds of the commandments and precepts of God are bound the kings of the Gentiles, the nobles of the world, by the weak and contemptible of this world, whom the Lord chose that he might confound all the strong things; and he filled these same with the Holy Ghost, and gave them two-edged swords, that they might turn the hearts of nobles to the fear of Christ, and that, worldly nobility being despised, they might choose poverty and nobility in Christ. For he willed to profit the emperor by a fisherman, not the fisherman by an emperor.

((AUG.)) By these he binds kings and nobles in iron *ferrcis* fetters, that they should not go forward to unlawful things.

notes.text: From our duty to magistrates he passes on to general duties. To love one another — An eternal debt, which can never be sufficiently discharged; but yet if this be rightly performed, it discharges all the rest. For he that loveth another - As he ought. Hath fulfilled the whole law - Toward his neighbour.

If there be any other — More particular. Commandment - Toward our neighbour; as there are many in the law. It is summed up in this - So that if you was not thinking of it, yet if your heart was full of love, you would fulfil it.
Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law — For the same love which restrains from all evil, incites us to all good.

And do this — Fulfil the law of love in all the instances above mentioned. Knowing the season - Full of grace, but hasting away. That it is high time to awake out of sleep - How beautifully is the metaphor carried on! This life, a night; the resurrection, the day; the gospel shining on the heart, the dawn of this day; we are to awake out of sleep; to rise up and throw away our night-clothes, fit only for darkness, and put on new; and, being soldiers, we are to arm, and prepare for fight, who are encompassed with so many enemies. The day dawns when we receive faith, and then sleep gives place. Then it is time to rise, to arm, to walk, to work, lest sleep steal upon us again. Final salvation, glory, is nearer to us now, than when we first believed - It is continually advancing, flying forward upon the swiftest wings of time. And that which remains between the present hour and eternity is comparatively but a moment.
Banqueting — Luxurious, elegant feasts.

But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ — Herein is contained the whole of our salvation. It is a strong and beautiful expression for the most intimate union with him, and being clothed with all the graces which were in him. The apostle does not say, Put on purity and sobriety, peacefulness and benevolence; but he says all this and a thousand times more at once, in saying, Put on Christ. And make not provision - To raise foolish desires, or, when they are raised already, to satisfy them.

glossa.text: *To no man anything.* Peace toward all, love among brethren. For otherwise they are not truly brethren. *That ye love.* Mention is made here of charity, because it avails unto this humility. For charity alone is that which, even when repaid, always keeps its debtor. For it is repaid when it is bestowed, but it is owed even if it has been repaid, because there is no time at which it is not to be bestowed. Nor when it is repaid is it lost, but rather it is multiplied by repaying; for it is repaid by having, not by lacking, as money which cannot be repaid unless it be had, nor be had unless it be repaid; nay rather, when it is repaid by a man, it grows in the man; and so much the greater is acquired, the more men it is repaid to. *He loveth his neighbor.* Since there are two precepts of charity, one is often put for both, because neither is God loved without the neighbor, nor the neighbor without God, nor can be. The love of the neighbor appears in deeds, the love of God lies more hidden, and therefore he sets down this one more particularly, of which the Lord says: *A new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another,* where that greater commandment of the love of God seems to be passed over. But by those who understand well, each is found in the other; because he who loves God cannot despise him whom God commands to be loved, and he who loves his neighbor holily and spiritually, what does he love in him but God? *His neighbor, hath fulfilled the law.* Every man must be understood by neighbor, because there is no one with whom evil is to be wrought. He therefore who loves men ought to love them either because they are just, or that they may be just. For so also he ought to love himself, namely, either because he is just, or that he may be just. For he who loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, because he loves himself to this end, that he may be unjust, therefore to this end, that he may be evil: therefore he no longer loves himself; for he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.

*And this knowing.* Namely, that it is the hour; or, as certain books have it: knowing this time, namely of grace. Now from the time when we have had love; it is the hour, that is, the opportunity, but a brief one. *To rise from sleep.* Sleep is negligence or ignorance. *For now.* Causes interposed, why we ought to rise. *Is nearer.* He that works well is near to eternal life. For baptism is unto pardon, a good life unto the crown. Or *nearer*, because we are more nigh to death.

*The night is past.* Again it is shown why they ought to rise: because the *night* of unbelief and ignorance *is past*, that is, has been; but now it is not, whose memory admonishes, that ye may beware. *But the day*, that is, eternal blessedness, *is at hand*, since sins are remitted, since ye are just through grace. The *night* is the old man, who passed away in baptism; the *day* is Christ the sun of justice, by whose light they have learned the truth, that they may know what is to be done. *The works of darkness.* Evil works, which have come out of the darkness of ignorance, or love the darkness, and lead to the darkness

*Not in rioting.* Note that in these things the Romans are touched; and therefore they have no right of boasting.

((AUG.)) But of these diseases pride is the mother, and the greediness of the human mind, which also often begets hypocrisy; this is not resisted, unless by frequent testimonies of the divine books fear and charity be struck in.

notes.text:
But how can we avoid giving offense to some? or being offended at others! Especially suppose they are quite in the wrong? Suppose they commit a known sin? Our Lord here teaches us how: he lays down a sure method of avoiding all offenses. Whosoever closely observes this threefold rule, will seldom offend others, and never be offended himself. If any do any thing amiss, of which thou art an eye or ear witness, thus saith the Lord, If thy brother — Any who is a member of the same religious community: Sin against thee,

1. Go and reprove him alone - If it may be in person; if that cannot so well be done, by thy messenger; or in writing. Observe, our Lord gives no liberty to omit this; or to exchange it for either of the following steps. If this do not succeed,

2. Take with thee one or two more - Men whom he esteems or loves, who may then confirm and enforce what thou sayest; and afterward, if need require, bear witness of what was spoken. If even this does not succeed, then, and not before,

3. Tell it to the elders of the Church - Lay the whole matter open before those who watch over yours and his soul. If all this avail not, have no farther intercourse with him, only such as thou hast with heathens. Can any thing be plainer? Christ does here as expressly command all Christians who see a brother do evil, to take this way, not another, and to take these steps, in this order, as he does to honour their father and mother. But if so, in what land do the Christians live? If we proceed from the private carriage of man to man, to proceedings of a more public nature, in what Christian nation are Church censures conformed to this rule? Is this the form in which ecclesiastical judgments appear, in the popish, or even the Protestant world? Are these the methods used even by those who boast the most loudly of the authority of Christ to confirm their sentences? Let us earnestly pray, that this dishonour to the Christian name may be wiped away, and that common humanity may not, with such solemn mockery, be destroyed in the name of the Lord! Let him be to thee as the heathen - To whom thou still owest earnest good will, and all the offices of humanity. Luke xvii, 3.

Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth — By excommunication, pronounced in the spirit and power of Christ. Whatsoever ye shall loose - By absolution from that sentence. In the primitive Church, absolution meant no more than a discharge from Church censure. Again I say - And not only your intercession for the penitent, but all your united prayers, shall be heard. How great then is the power of joint prayer! If two of you - Suppose a man and his wife. Matt. xvi, 19.
Where two or three are gathered together in my name — That is, to worship me. I am in the midst of them - By my Spirit, to quicken their prayers, guide their counsels, and answer their petitions.

glossa.text: *But if he shall offend against thee,* etc. For if against God, it is not in our judgment. In this order we ought to shun scandals, that we hurt no one: and that we rebuke the sinner with a zeal for justice, and open the bowels of mercy to him that repents. *Rebuke him,* etc. He does not bid us forgive the sinner indiscriminately; but him that repents. He sins thus, who seeing his brother sin keeps silent: as does he who does not pardon the penitent. For what he said, "if he repents, forgive," he prefaced by "if he shall have sinned, rebuke." Let pardon be neither hard, nor indulgence slack.

*Tell the Church.* That it may hold him in detestation, etc., *as far as* they are condemned, that a human sentence is confirmed by the divine sentence. *As the heathen.* More detestable is he who acts under the name of a believer, etc., *as far as* through thefts and through perjuries.
*Amen I say,* etc. So far is your sentence confirmed by the divine, whether for receiving the penitent, or for casting off the obstinate.

*If two.* Typically. Where the spirit, the soul and the body have agreed, so that there is no war between them, the flesh lusting against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, whatsoever they ask shall be done. Because if the body wills what the spirit wills, the asking is only for good things. *There am I in me.* That is, every discourse calls to concord and to the peace which he so far commends that he says God is in the midst of them, because peace and charity set up their seat in the peaceable, and he affirms that by the merit of unity all things that are to be asked are to be obtained.

notes.text: Our sins — The unpardoned guilt, and the unsupportable punishment of our sins, in the wasting of our country, burning our city, abolishing the publick worship of God; we shall pine away, 'tis too late to hope. How - How can it be better with us?

Covetousness — He mentions this in particular, because it is most opposite to God's testimonies, and does most commonly hinder men from receiving his word, and from profiting by it: and because it is most pernicious, as being the root of all evil.
Vanity — The vain things of this present world, such as riches, honours, pleasures: from beholding them, with desire or affection. Quicken - Make me lively, vigourous and fervent in thy service.
Stablish — Confirm and perform thy promises.
I fear — For my instability in thy ways; which in respect to my own weakness, I have great cause to fear.
Longed — After a more solid knowledge and constant performance of them. In - According to thy faithfulness.

And make not provision - To raise foolish desires, or, when they are raised already, to satisfy them.

glossa.text: *To no man anything.* Peace toward all, love among brethren. For otherwise they are not truly brethren. *That ye love.* Mention is made here of charity, because it avails unto this humility. For charity alone is that which, even when repaid, always keeps its debtor. For it is repaid when it is bestowed, but it is owed even if it has been repaid, because there is no time at which it is not to be bestowed. Nor when it is repaid is it lost, but rather it is multiplied by repaying; for it is repaid by having, not by lacking, as money which cannot be repaid unless it be had, nor be had unless it be repaid; nay rather, when it is repaid by a man, it grows in the man; and so much the greater is acquired, the more men it is repaid to. *He loveth his neighbor.* Since there are two precepts of charity, one is often put for both, because neither is God loved without the neighbor, nor the neighbor without God, nor can be. The love of the neighbor appears in deeds, the love of God lies more hidden, and therefore he sets down this one more particularly, of which the Lord says: *A new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another,* where that greater commandment of the love of God seems to be passed over. But by those who understand well, each is found in the other; because he who loves God cannot despise him whom God commands to be loved, and he who loves his neighbor holily and spiritually, what does he love in him but God? *His neighbor, hath fulfilled the law.* Every man must be understood by neighbor, because there is no one with whom evil is to be wrought. He therefore who loves men ought to love them either because they are just, or that they may be just. For so also he ought to love himself, namely, either because he is just, or that he may be just. For he who loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, because he loves himself to this end, that he may be unjust, therefore to this end, that he may be evil: therefore he no longer loves himself; for he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.

*And this knowing.* Namely, that it is the hour; or, as certain books have it: knowing this time, namely of grace. Now from the time when we have had love; it is the hour, that is, the opportunity, but a brief one. *To rise from sleep.* Sleep is negligence or ignorance. *For now.* Causes interposed, why we ought to rise. *Is nearer.* He that works well is near to eternal life. For baptism is unto pardon, a good life unto the crown. Or *nearer*, because we are more nigh to death.

*The night is past.* Again it is shown why they ought to rise: because the *night* of unbelief and ignorance *is past*, that is, has been; but now it is not, whose memory admonishes, that ye may beware. *But the day*, that is, eternal blessedness, *is at hand*, since sins are remitted, since ye are just through grace. The *night* is the old man, who passed away in baptism; the *day* is Christ the sun of justice, by whose light they have learned the truth, that they may know what is to be done. *The works of darkness.* Evil works, which have come out of the darkness of ignorance, or love the darkness, and lead to the darkness

*Not in rioting.* Note that in these things the Romans are touched; and therefore they have no right of boasting.

((AUG.)) But of these diseases pride is the mother, and the greediness of the human mind, which also often begets hypocrisy; this is not resisted, unless by frequent testimonies of the divine books fear and charity be struck in.

notes.text:
But how can we avoid giving offense to some? or being offended at others! Especially suppose they are quite in the wrong? Suppose they commit a known sin? Our Lord here teaches us how: he lays down a sure method of avoiding all offenses. Whosoever closely observes this threefold rule, will seldom offend others, and never be offended himself. If any do any thing amiss, of which thou art an eye or ear witness, thus saith the Lord, If thy brother — Any who is a member of the same religious community: Sin against thee,

1. Go and reprove him alone - If it may be in person; if that cannot so well be done, by thy messenger; or in writing. Observe, our Lord gives no liberty to omit this; or to exchange it for either of the following steps. If this do not succeed,

2. Take with thee one or two more - Men whom he esteems or loves, who may then confirm and enforce what thou sayest; and afterward, if need require, bear witness of what was spoken. If even this does not succeed, then, and not before,

3. Tell it to the elders of the Church - Lay the whole matter open before those who watch over yours and his soul. If all this avail not, have no farther intercourse with him, only such as thou hast with heathens. Can any thing be plainer? Christ does here as expressly command all Christians who see a brother do evil, to take this way, not another, and to take these steps, in this order, as he does to honour their father and mother. But if so, in what land do the Christians live? If we proceed from the private carriage of man to man, to proceedings of a more public nature, in what Christian nation are Church censures conformed to this rule? Is this the form in which ecclesiastical judgments appear, in the popish, or even the Protestant world? Are these the methods used even by those who boast the most loudly of the authority of Christ to confirm their sentences? Let us earnestly pray, that this dishonour to the Christian name may be wiped away, and that common humanity may not, with such solemn mockery, be destroyed in the name of the Lord! Let him be to thee as the heathen - To whom thou still owest earnest good will, and all the offices of humanity. Luke xvii, 3.

Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth — By excommunication, pronounced in the spirit and power of Christ. Whatsoever ye shall loose - By absolution from that sentence. In the primitive Church, absolution meant no more than a discharge from Church censure. Again I say - And not only your intercession for the penitent, but all your united prayers, shall be heard. How great then is the power of joint prayer! If two of you - Suppose a man and his wife. Matt. xvi, 19.
Where two or three are gathered together in my name — That is, to worship me. I am in the midst of them - By my Spirit, to quicken their prayers, guide their counsels, and answer their petitions.

glossa.text: *But if he shall offend against thee,* etc. For if against God, it is not in our judgment. In this order we ought to shun scandals, that we hurt no one: and that we rebuke the sinner with a zeal for justice, and open the bowels of mercy to him that repents. *Rebuke him,* etc. He does not bid us forgive the sinner indiscriminately; but him that repents. He sins thus, who seeing his brother sin keeps silent: as does he who does not pardon the penitent. For what he said, "if he repents, forgive," he prefaced by "if he shall have sinned, rebuke." Let pardon be neither hard, nor indulgence slack.

*Tell the Church.* That it may hold him in detestation, etc., *as far as* they are condemned, that a human sentence is confirmed by the divine sentence. *As the heathen.* More detestable is he who acts under the name of a believer, etc., *as far as* through thefts and through perjuries.
*Amen I say,* etc. So far is your sentence confirmed by the divine, whether for receiving the penitent, or for casting off the obstinate.

*If two.* Typically. Where the spirit, the soul and the body have agreed, so that there is no war between them, the flesh lusting against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, whatsoever they ask shall be done. Because if the body wills what the spirit wills, the asking is only for good things. *There am I in me.* That is, every discourse calls to concord and to the peace which he so far commends that he says God is in the midst of them, because peace and charity set up their seat in the peaceable, and he affirms that by the merit of unity all things that are to be asked are to be obtained.

turn.gravity: Israel marks the Passover with blood on the doorposts, the sign that turns death aside (Exodus 12); Paul reduces the whole law to one debt that's never paid off — "owe no one anything, except to love one another" (Romans 13); and Jesus gives a specific procedure for confronting sin in the community — private first, then witnesses, then the whole church. The nerve: love for the offender, not exposure of the offender, drives every step of the process.
turn.trap: Becomes a weapon (church discipline as public shaming, or a rulebook for cutting someone off) or is avoided altogether ("just forgive and forget," skip the confrontation) — missing that the goal named at each step is to *gain* the brother, not to win an argument.
turn.hinge: The process ends in a possible verdict of "let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector" — yet Jesus spent his whole ministry eating with Gentiles and tax collectors. The most severe thing this text allows is: treat him like someone I would still go find.

doors.claim: Confrontation begins one-on-one, in private, because shame compounds sin rather than curing it.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Thy brother is to be reproved in private, lest if once he has lost a sense of shame, he should continue in sin.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Our Lord admonishes us not to overlook one another's faults, yet not so as seeking for matter of blame, but watching what you may amend.

doors.say: The first move is never public — not because sin should be hidden, but because shame, once a person loses it, stops correcting anything.
doors.do: Ask them to name someone they're tempted to expose rather than approach, and go to that person alone first.

doors.claim: Reconciliation is a gain for both people, not a victory for one — the goal reframes confrontation as rescue, not conquest.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He said not, he has gained himself, but, you have gained him; which shews that both of you are the gainers.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: For in saving another, salvation is gained for ourselves also.

doors.say: When you go to confront someone, you're not just trying to fix them — you're trying to get both of you back.
doors.do: Have them reframe one grievance they're holding as a potential mutual gain, not a case to win.

doors.landing: Like a Gentile and a tax collector
doors.claim: The harshest verdict this text allows is to treat someone the way Jesus treated Gentiles and tax collectors — which is to say, still pursued, still eaten with, never written off.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: That He says, 'As a heathen and a publican,' shews that he is to be more abhorred, who under the name of a believer does the deeds of an unbeliever.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Though even thus we are not to neglect his salvation; for the heathens themselves, that is, the gentiles...

doors.say: Even the worst verdict in this text isn't exile — it's the status Jesus spent his whole ministry crossing over to reach.
doors.do: Ask them to name someone they've functionally written off, and identify one way Jesus would still be pursuing that person.

synthesis.convergence: Passover blood marks a door so death passes over, not so the household is exposed (Exodus 12); Paul reduces every commandment to one unpaid debt — love (Romans 13); and Jesus' whole procedure for confronting sin aims at gathering back in, ending in the promise that where two or three gather in his name, he is there. Every reading refuses a religion of exposure for a religion of restoration.
synthesis.claim: The point of naming what's wrong is never exposure — it's the door left open for someone to come back through.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that either weaponizes accountability or avoids it entirely, name the actual goal Jesus gives: not being right, not being safe from confrontation, but gaining each other back.

turn.subtract: Three landings — the private first step, the mutual gain, or what the harshest verdict actually permits. Choose one and let the others go.
turn.source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
